title: MoSA: Learning Residual Stress for Better Robot Dynamics
one_liner: Start with a standard physics model, then learn what it got wrong about how real materials deform, using the material's own motion to guide the correction.
lead: Robots learn to move objects by watching videos and building a mental model of how things deform. But physics simulators assume all materials act the same way in every direction — that is not true. Real materials bend differently along different axes. This paper fixes it by keeping the standard simulator as a foundation and learning to add the missing irregularities.

problem.h2: Standard physics simulators miss the quirks of real materials
paras: A physics simulator tells a robot how a cloth or foam will move when pushed. It assumes materials are homogeneous (the same throughout) and isotropic (the same in every direction). A real rubber band does not work that way — it stretches differently along its length than across its width.

If you start with a good isotropic model, the remaining error comes from these directional quirks. A naive approach would throw away the physics model and train a neural network to predict raw motion from scratch. But neural networks then waste data learning obvious physics laws instead of learning the weird residual effects, and they overfit to the training videos.

callout.html: Keep the standard isotropic simulator, but train a small neural network to learn and add the missing directional stress corrections.

steps.text: Begin with the standard isotropic constitutive model (stress-strain relationship) — the foundation that already captures most real behavior.
Small neural networks learn residual stress operators that adjust the base prediction step by step.
Directly supervise how the deformation field changes over time and space (its derivatives).
Compare rendered predictions against actual video frames pixel by pixel.
The correction networks learn the exact directional quirks needed to close the gap.

paras: The paper modifies the stress operator — the mapping from how much a material has stretched (strain) to how much it pushes back (stress). Normally this is fixed by physics. Here, the paper learns small corrections to it that capture real-world anisotropy.

hidden.h2: Residual anisotropy: how directional is the material
hidden.name: residual anisotropy
paras: Anisotropy means a material behaves differently in different directions. A perfect isotropic material has zero anisotropy. Real materials have small but measurable anisotropy — a rubber band is stiffer along its length than across.

The paper measures this by looking at what the standard isotropic model got wrong. After training, the learned residual stress operators encode exactly this anisotropy. The paper validates that the model truly learned the material's directional properties by checking whether the learned corrections transfer to new materials and by verifying the corrections match expected physics patterns.

heat.caption: Darker means stronger anisotropy or heterogeneity; highlights show where the learned corrections matter most.

reads.html: A material's anisotropy is how much it bends differently along different axes. The paper learns this by letting small neural networks adjust the standard physics model until predictions match real videos.
Residual stress operators capture mild anisotropy and heterogeneity via microplane-constrained redistribution in a physics-informed cascaded network.

mechanism.h2: Why learning residual stress fixes the real-to-sim gap
paras: A standard physics model assumes isotropy because it is mathematically simple. Most of the real behavior is isotropic, so this assumption is almost right. The gap comes from the small directional and spatial quirks. Trying to fit all of this from scratch with a neural network wastes data and overfits because the model has to re-learn all the isotropic physics from videos.

Instead, the paper keeps the isotropic model as a scaffold. Small neural networks then learn ONLY the corrections on top. This is much more efficient because the heavy lifting (isotropy) is already done. The motion constraints (supervising the deformation field's time and space derivatives) push the corrections toward physically realistic patterns instead of memorizing rendering accidents. The cascade structure (applying corrections step-by-step) forces the model to decompose the anisotropy and heterogeneity into interpretable pieces, so the learned corrections actually represent real material properties instead of noise.

stages.s: Video of deformation + initial isotropic prediction
Neural network 1: pre-correction to base stress
Motion constraints: supervise derivatives to enforce physics
Final stress with learned residual anisotropy

math.h2: Equation: corrected stress from isotropic base
math.words: Final stress equals: isotropic stress, then apply a learned pre-correction, then redistribute across directions (microplane), then apply a learned post-correction and rescaling. Optionally add a learned heterogeneity term.
symbols: the stress from the standard isotropic model
learned pre-correction network (adjusts magnitude before redistribution)
microplane-based redistribution (changes how stress points in different directions)
learned scaling factors (how much each direction's correction matters)
learned heterogeneity term (spatial non-uniformity within the material)
the final stress with residual anisotropy accounted for

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Say isotropic model predicts stress = 50 (in some direction).
Microplane redistribution rotates stress ellipse: some directions get +10, others get -5.
Post-correction learns to scale by 1.1 and add 2 -> first direction 57, second 40.5.
Heterogeneity adds local spatial variation: +3 in this zone -> first direction 60, second 43.5.
Result: isotropic base corrected with learned directional quirks.

math.note: The cascade of corrections (pre, redistribute, post, heterogeneity) decomposes the residual error into interpretable pieces so each part learns real material properties.

bars.h2: Comparison: isotropic model vs. isotropic plus learned residuals

charts.title: Standard isotropic physics
charts.note: Isotropic model fits training well but misses directional quirks on new data and drifts over time.

charts.title: Isotropic plus learned residuals (MoSA)
charts.note: Learned corrections close the gap on unseen videos and keep predictions stable for longer simulations.

items.b: Too much freedom in the correction networks.
items.html: If the neural networks are too large, they can overfit to the training video instead of learning real material properties. Motion constraints prevent this because they directly supervise how the material moves through time and space — rendering artifacts do not obey real motion laws, so enforcing physics on the motion derivatives rules out overfitting solutions. The cascade structure prevents overfitting because it forces the corrections to decompose into stages, so memorizing one piece breaks the whole pipeline unless that piece corresponds to real physical behavior.

items.b: Material changes between training and deployment.
items.html: If you learn residual stress on rubber but then deploy on leather, the learned corrections do not transfer. The paper validates transfer by testing on different materials and shows good generalization when the materials are similar.
If the deformation video is blurry or low-res, the motion constraint supervision (tracking spatial and temporal derivatives) becomes noisy and the model learns spurious corrections.

With proper supervision from high-quality video, a good starting isotropic physics model, and motion constraints, the learned residuals capture genuine material anisotropy and transfer to new scenarios.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulator that learns dynamics from video. First, train it on 20 frames of cloth or foam deforming. Then predict the next 10 frames without seeing them. Measure how closely the predictions match the actual video (pixel-by-pixel similarity). Show that the isotropic model makes smooth but directionally wrong predictions, and that MoSA's learned residuals fix the directional errors. Finally, take the learned residuals from one material and try applying them to a different material — show that they do not blindly transfer, proving the model learned real properties, not rendering artifacts.
demo.metric_eq: prediction_accuracy = average pixel similarity over 10 unseen frames; stability = how much prediction error grows from frame 5 to frame 10
demo.closing: The demo must show that isotropic-plus-residuals outperforms pure isotropic on directional accuracy because the residuals capture real anisotropy that isotropy misses, and outperforms pure neural networks on generalization because learning only the residuals (not re-deriving isotropy from scratch) forces the network to find real material properties instead of memorizing training patterns.
